english: My name is Oleg.
tip: To give your name, Russian says зовут (zavut = they call) plus you in the object form: меня (menya = me). It reads 'me they-call'.

english: During the day I work.
tip: днём (dnyom = in the daytime) is the instrumental form used for time of day; the -ём (-yom) ending means 'during', no preposition needed.

english: What time is it now?
tip: To ask the time, Russian says который час (katoryy chas = which hour), literally 'which hour', not 'what time'.

english: I love my family.
tip: свою (svayu = one's own) points back to the subject, so it fits any person. Use it, not мою (mayu = my), when the owner is the subject.

english: I speak Russian well.
tip: To say you speak a language, use the по- adverb: по-русски (pa-russki = in Russian). Lowercase and hyphenated, not the noun form.

english: I recently read a book.
tip: Past-tense verbs agree with the speaker's gender: a woman says читала (chitala = read), a man says читал (chital).

english: Grandmother doesn't have a phone.
tip: нет (net = there isn't) forces the next noun into the genitive: телефона (telefona = of a phone). It marks the missing thing.

english: She writes with her left hand.
tip: The tool you use goes in the instrumental with no preposition: левой рукой (levay rukoy = with the left hand). The -ой (-oy) ending means 'by means of'.

english: What time does the museum close?
tip: The -ся (-sya) on закрывается (zakryvaetsya = closes) makes it happen by itself; the museum does not close something, it just closes.

english: I write a letter to a friend.
tip: The person you write to goes in the dative: другу (drugu = to a friend). No separate word for 'to'; the -у (-u) ending carries it.

english: I am looking for a good dentist.
tip: For an animate male object, accusative copies the genitive: хорошего стоматолога (kharosheva stamatolaga = a good dentist). The -его/-а (-eva/-a) endings mark it.

english: She asked what I do.
tip: заниматься (zanimat'sya = to be occupied with) takes the instrumental, so 'what' becomes чем (chem): чем я занимаюсь (chem ya zanimayus' = what I do).

english: Grandmother is eighty-five years old.
tip: Age puts the person in the dative and drops the verb 'to be': бабушке (babushke = to grandmother) is eighty-five, literally 'to grandmother 85'.

english: She came to work early.
tip: Motion toward uses на (na) plus accusative: пришла на работу (prishla na rabotu = came to work); staying there is на работе (na rabote).

english: I'm not cold, I'm hot.
tip: Feeling hot or cold uses the dative and no verb 'to be': мне (mne = to me) жарко (zharka = hot) means 'I am hot'.

english: We waited for about two hours.
tip: около (okala = about) gives an approximate time or amount and takes the genitive: около двух часов (okala dvukh chasov = about two hours).

english: What time is it? Ten to two.
tip: Minutes 'to' the hour use без (bez = without) plus the genitive: без десяти два (bez desyati dva = ten to two), literally 'without ten, two'.

target: Зачем же ты столько хлеба накупил?
english: Why did you buy so much bread?
tip: Quantity words take the genitive: столько хлеба (stolka khleba = so much bread), not the plain form хлеб (khleb).

target: Я знаю человека, который это сделал.
english: I know the person who did this.
tip: который (katoryy = who) takes its gender from человека (chelaveka = person) but its case from its own clause, here subject, so nominative.

target: Она доехала до работы за час.
english: She got to work in an hour.
tip: To say how long an action took to finish, use за (za = in) plus the accusative: за час (za chas = in an hour).

english: I've been waiting for half an hour already.
tip: For an action still going on, Russian keeps the present where English uses 'have been': жду уже (zhdu uzhe = I've already been waiting).

english: What do you need so much money for?
tip: зачем (zachem = what for) asks about purpose, while почему (pachemu = why) asks about cause. Here it means 'what do you need it for'.

english: Our wedding is on the second of February.
tip: A date you do something 'on' takes the genitive: второго февраля (vtarova fevralya = on the second of February). No word for 'on' needed.

target: Пока я ждал автобус, читал газету.
english: While I was waiting for the bus, I read the newspaper.
tip: пока (paka = while) pairs with imperfective verbs for two things at once: ждал (zhdal = was waiting), читал (chital = was reading).

english: The programmer is going to work now.
tip: едет (edet = is riding) is one trip happening right now; ездит (ezdit = rides) would mean regular, repeated trips.

target: Книга, которую я прочитал, стоит на полке.
english: The book that I read is on the shelf.
tip: которую (katoruyu = which) is feminine to match книга (kniga = book), but accusative because it is the object of прочитал (prachital = read).

english: There are four books on the table.
tip: After 2, 3, 4 the noun is genitive singular, not plural: четыре книги (chetyre knigi = four books).

target: Правда ли, что завтра будет снег?
english: Is it true that it will snow tomorrow?
tip: ли turns a statement into a yes/no question and attaches to the word being asked about: правда ли (pravda li = is it true).

target: Она работает врачом в городской больнице.
english: She works as a doctor at the city hospital.
tip: Working 'as' a profession uses the instrumental: работает врачом (rabotaet vrachom = works as a doctor). The -ом (-om) ending replaces 'as a'.

target: Я играю в парке по выходным.
english: I play in the park on weekends.
tip: For 'on' recurring days, use по (pa) plus the dative: по выходным (pa vykhadnym = on weekends). It marks a repeated schedule.
